pos: proper n. (king of Ethiopia in the days of Hezekiah)
etymology: Hebrew tirhaqah, rendering the Egyptian-Kushite royal name known from the monuments as Taharqa.
biblical_def: Tirhakah appears at the height of Sennacherib's campaign against Judah. While the Assyrian army pressed Hezekiah, a report came north: “And when he heard say of Tirhakah king of Ethiopia, Behold, he is come out to fight against thee: he sent messengers again unto Hezekiah” (2 Kings 19:9). Isaiah records the same moment (Isaiah 37:9). Tirhakah was the Kushite pharaoh of Egypt's twenty-fifth dynasty, and Judah's politicians had long trusted in Egypt and Ethiopia for rescue. But the deliverance of Jerusalem did not come from Tirhakah's march. It came from heaven: “And it came to pass that night, that the angel of the LORD went out, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians an hundred fourscore and five thousand” (2 Kings 19:35). The Ethiopian king is a footnote in the story, and that is the lesson. The arm of flesh moved, and God did not need it.

corruption_summary: Critics once used Tirhakah's title as proof of a scribal blunder, when the monuments show the writer knew exactly whom he named.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Taharqa became sole king of Egypt only around 690 BC, a decade after Sennacherib's campaign of 701, critical scholarship long charged 2 Kings with an anachronism. Further study of the inscriptions showed Taharqa active as a royal prince and commander in that period, and the text calls him king in the natural way of a writer naming the man by the title he was known by.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the narrative is history, and that its point is theological: Judah was saved not by Egypt and Ethiopia but by the LORD, as Isaiah had warned them to trust Him rather than the horses of Egypt.

pos: proper n. (king of Assyria who besieged Samaria)
etymology: Hebrew shalman'eser, from the Akkadian royal name Shulmanu-asharedu, the god Shulmanu is foremost; the king of 2 Kings 17 and 18 is Shalmaneser V.
biblical_def: Shalmaneser was the instrument of the northern kingdom's end. Hoshea, Israel's last king, first submitted and paid tribute, then conspired with Egypt, and the Assyrian came against him. “And it came to pass in the fourth year of king Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, that Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria, and besieged it” (2 Kings 18:9). After three years the city fell, and the people were carried into exile (2 Kings 18:11). But the historian will not let the reader rest in politics. The cause is stated plainly: “Because they obeyed not the voice of the LORD their God, but transgressed his covenant, and all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded” (2 Kings 18:12). Shalmaneser besieged Samaria; the covenant curse brought it down.

corruption_paragraphs: Ancient Near Eastern history rightly reconstructs Assyria's westward expansion, tribute system and deportations. The danger is to stop there and treat the prophets' verdict as pious decoration on a political event. The Chronicler and the writer of Kings give the theological verdict as the real explanation, and the dictionary follows it.

pos: proper n. (king of Babylon who released Jehoiachin)
etymology: Hebrew 'evil merodakh, from the Akkadian Amel-Marduk, man of Marduk. The English look of the first syllable is accidental and has nothing to do with evil.
biblical_def: The book of Kings closes not with the fall of Jerusalem but with a small mercy in Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar's son came to the throne in 562 BC, and in his first year he showed kindness to the captive king of Judah. Jeremiah's book ends the same way: “that Evilmerodach king of Babylon in the first year of his reign lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, and brought him forth out of prison” (Jeremiah 52:31). He “spake kindly unto him, and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon” (Jeremiah 52:32), and Jehoiachin “did continually eat bread before him all the days of his life” (Jeremiah 52:33). After thirty-seven years in prison, David's heir sat at a king's table. It was a thread, not a restoration; but the thread was the line of David, and God had sworn to keep it.

Placed at the very end of Kings and of Jeremiah, it is a deliberate word of hope. Ration tablets from Babylon list Jehoiachin, king of Judah, among those receiving provisions, a striking corroboration of the account.

pos: proper n. (son and murderer of Sennacherib)
etymology: Hebrew shar'etser, from an Akkadian name ending -shar-usur, protect the king. A different man from Nergalsharezer of Jeremiah 39.
biblical_def: Sharezer's single act fulfilled a prophecy. When Sennacherib blasphemed the living God before Jerusalem, the LORD said through Isaiah: “Behold, I will send a blast upon him, and he shall hear a rumour, and shall return to his own land; and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own land” (2 Kings 19:7). The army was struck, the king went home, and years later the word was finished in a temple: “as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 19:37). The man who asked which god had delivered any nation out of the hand of Assyria died before his own god, at the hands of his own sons.

etymology: Hebrew tartan, from the Akkadian turtanu, the title of the supreme commander of the Assyrian army, second to the king. The Authorized Version prints it as a name.
biblical_def: The Tartan appears at the head of the embassy that came to frighten Jerusalem: “And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem” (2 Kings 18:17). All three are titles: the commander-in-chief, the chief officer, and the chief cupbearer. Isaiah had already dated a prophecy by an earlier Tartan's campaign: “In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it” (Isaiah 20:1). Isaiah then walked barefoot three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 20:3), warning Judah not to lean on the nations Assyria's Tartan was about to humble. The office was the sharpest sword of the greatest empire on earth, and both times the Scripture names it, the lesson is to trust the LORD rather than the powers.

pos: proper n. (one of the four kings of Genesis 14)
etymology: Hebrew tid'al, commonly compared with the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya. He is called king of nations, Hebrew goyim.
biblical_def: Tidal belongs to the first war recorded in Scripture. “And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations” (Genesis 14:1). The four eastern kings crushed the five kings of the plain, “four kings with five” (Genesis 14:9), and carried off Lot. Abram armed his trained servants, pursued by night, and recovered all. Then Melchizedek met him with bread and wine and blessed him: “And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all” (Genesis 14:20). Tidal and his allies were the mightiest men Abram ever faced, and Scripture records their names chiefly so that the victory may be ascribed to God, and Abram's tithe to God's priest.

pos: proper n. (son of Herod the Great, ruler of Judaea)
etymology: Greek Archelaos, from archo, to rule, and laos, people: ruler of the people.
biblical_def: Archelaus is named once, and the mention turns the steps of the holy family. When Herod the Great died, the angel told Joseph in Egypt to return to Israel (Matthew 2:19). “But when he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither: notwithstanding, being warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into the parts of Galilee” (Matthew 2:22). Archelaus was Herod's son and his match in cruelty, and Rome removed him in AD 6 after complaints from his own subjects. Joseph's fear was well founded, but it was God's warning that settled the road: “And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matthew 2:23). A tyrant's accession became the means by which the Christ grew up despised in Galilee.

pos: proper n. (king of the Nabataean Arabs)
etymology: Greek Aretas, from the Nabataean royal name Haritat; the king of 2 Corinthians 11:32 is Aretas IV, who reigned about 9 BC to AD 40.
biblical_def: Paul names Aretas in the catalogue of his weaknesses, in the very place where a boaster would have hidden the story. “In Damascus the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me: And through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands” (2 Corinthians 11:32-33). Luke tells the same night from the other side: “Then the disciples took him by night, and let him down by the wall in a basket” (Acts 9:25). The great apostle's first exit from a city as a preacher of Christ was through a window, in a basket, in the dark. Paul glories in it precisely because it is humbling: “If I must needs glory, I will glory of the things which concern mine infirmities” (2 Corinthians 11:30). The king's garrison is remembered only because it could not hold the man God meant to send.

pos: proper n. (Roman governor of Syria at the taxing of Luke 2)
etymology: Greek Kyrenios, the Greek form of the Latin Quirinius: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, Roman consul and legate of Syria.
biblical_def: Luke ties the birth of Christ to the machinery of Rome. “And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed” (Luke 2:1). He adds a note to fix the time: “And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria” (Luke 2:2). The registration sent Joseph and Mary from Nazareth “unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem” (Luke 2:4), and so an emperor's decree carried the Virgin to the town Micah had named seven centuries before. Cyrenius never knew what his census accomplished. He was counting subjects for Caesar; God was bringing His Son to be born where the prophet said.

corruption_summary: Luke is charged with a chronological blunder over Cyrenius, when the verse itself and the record of Quirinius' career admit an honest and accurate reading.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical scholarship has long held that Luke confused the census of Quirinius in AD 6 with the birth of Jesus before Herod's death in 4 BC. But Luke knew of the AD 6 census (Acts 5:37), and he carefully calls this one the first, which may be rendered before Quirinius was governor. Quirinius also held earlier commands in the region. Luke, whom the archaeologist William Ramsay came to honour as a historian of the first rank, is to be trusted, not corrected.
The dictionary reads Scripture as true history. The principle to recover is providence over empires: the decree of Augustus served the birth of the Son of David in Bethlehem, as God had foretold.

pos: proper n. (tetrarch of Abilene in the fifteenth year of Tiberius)
etymology: Greek Lysanias, from lusis, a loosing, and ania, sorrow: ending sorrow.
biblical_def: Lysanias is one name in the most carefully dated sentence in the Gospels. “Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judaea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luke 3:1). Luke continues: “Annas and Caiaphas being the high priests, the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2). The emperor, the governor, three tetrarchs and two high priests are all lined up so that one thing may be placed in time: the word of God came to a man in the desert. The powers are named; the word is what matters. And John went preaching “the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins” (Luke 3:3).

corruption_summary: Lysanias was the textbook case of Luke's supposed error, until an inscription from Abila named a tetrarch Lysanias in exactly Luke's period.
corruption_paragraphs: Critics pointed out that the well-known Lysanias, king of Chalcis, was executed in 36 BC, and concluded that Luke had blundered by sixty years. An inscription found at Abila, dated to the reign of Tiberius, mentions Lysanias the tetrarch, confirming a later ruler of that name. The supposed error was the critics', not Luke's.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reliability of the inspired historian. Luke wrote that Theophilus might know the certainty of the things wherein he had been instructed, and he has repeatedly been proved right where he was charged with error.
